utterances.text: Well, he goes on to say that it was for this reason that we signed an agreement, called in the international forces as soon as we were able to do that, and over the many years of fighting and struggles, where nothing bore fruit, we finally gained the right, with Operations Flash and Storm, to liberate two areas of occupied Croatia. And once the opportunity arose for Eastern Slavonia to follow suit, this area here [indicates], to have Eastern Slavonia peacefully come under the authority of Croatia. Franjo Tudjman agreed, and General Klein, together with the Croatian leadership, performed the task, and I think the United Nations can be proud of the first such successful operation in its history, although there were calls to undertake military action to liberate the area, to make up for Vukovar, if I can put it that way, or to show that we were able to bring Vukovar back to the fold in this way. But, anyway, if something could be done peacefully, then that was the option. We were never for a military option, and that includes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here I would like to provide a piece of information to the Trial Chamber. We're talking of the pre-historical spirit, about destruction in Croatia. On page 22 of "The Croatian Soldier," it says here that there were 854 settlements in Croatia that came under attack, and around 5.000 individual monuments, historical edifices, and monuments and historical settlements were destroyed. And what follows is a list of all of that. It was not only Croatian settlements and monuments that were destroyed, but also the Czech, the Ukraine, and the Hungarian culture and historical monuments as well, and nothing remains of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are moving to 3D01297. That's the next document that I would like to discuss, under the title "Let's Win With the Good." In Croatian, this is 3D29-0642, and the English version number is -- I can't find it at the moment. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. I'll come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author is Zvonko Knezovic, a psychologist employed at the IPD. There were hundreds of psychologists who educated the Croatian Army in stress prevention and other things that were relevant for them. One of them was Mr. Knezovic. I would like to demonstrate the ideology behind our thoughts on war. He says that Croats should not fall into the trap of those who want to humiliate them by induced Ustasha movement; in other words, many who listened about Yugoslavia as an excellent country. And the fifth is simply use the media to transform Croats, including myself, into some sort of Ustasha, and that's how this was received. And in this text, he simply says, Let's use good to win. We mustn't be like them. And he says that's the position of the whole department through which hundreds of psychologists were employed to work all over Croatia in all the battle-fields and battle-fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. There must have been a technical hiccup. We have not been able to locate the translation of this page. Something has occurred, and I can't display the page. I apologise. However, can the General please proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel, I think, actually, I've got it. We're looking at an article by General -- well, I'm looking at something called "Discipline, A Mighty Weapon." Maybe I'm in the wrong place. What's the name of the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The article that you're looking at is "Let's Win Through Goodness." The article that you're looking at is the translation of the previous article that General Praljak has not commented upon. What he is commenting upon now is "Let's Win Through Goodness," and the author is Zvonko Knezevic. You will find his name in the right upper-hand corner. I'm not able to find the translation, which doesn't exclude --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I believe that I provided the gist of the text, and you will subsequently provide the number. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I was going to say. Let's move on, and we'll come back to the number of this text in English later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to move on to 3D01299. That's the next article that I would like to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title is "Why Did Serbia Accept a Cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this is 3D29-0650 in e-court, the English version -- the Croatia version, and the English version is 3D36-0758 through 0761. Go on, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general is -- Davor Butkovic is the author, and he mentions a few things here. The first one is that Serbia accepted a cease-fire under the conditions that it did not find suitable. The acceptance of the cease-fire is contrary to their goals and their fall-back position to these goals. Further on, he says that the cease-fire affected the rebels and insurgents, which is corroborated by Milan Babic's reaction. Milan Babic was surprised to see that Cyrus Vance did not want to talk to them, and they claim that the arrival of peacekeeping forces in crisis areas was not acceptable. Obviously, Hadzic, who was the ruler around Vukovar, harboured different political options, and he goes on to say that Croatia waged and won the war on two different levels; the first one was a diplomatic level, and the other one was a military level. And I quote: "Through clever and patient negotiation, Dr. Franjo Tudjman managed to re-establish complete and undeniable Croatian statehood after 900 years, thereby creating a precondition for the cease-fire." And he goes on to say that the Croatian Army takes credit for that, for having repelled the attacks. It demonstrated that it was impossible to defeat a people that was defending itself. Further on, he says that the Yugoslav Army, before the all-out conflict, was a hundred times more powerful than the Croatian units at the time. Towards the end of the paragraph, it says here we did not have tanks, we did not have heavy artillery, we did not have anti-aircraft defence systems, and so on and so forth, there was very little ammunition, and most of our soldiers were members of the police forces, where their commanders were often Serbian spies. He goes on to speak about the personnel policy pursued by Franjo Tudjman and says that there are three reasons why the Croatian Army was established so quickly: first of all, after the aggression against Slovenia, which marked the end of any sort of Yugoslavia, a lot of the best officers of the Yugoslav People's Army crossed over to our side. The Yugoslav Army at that moment did not have a single officer, save for General Kadijevic; a war criminal, General Mladic, whose military abilities were on par with those of General Tus, Spegelj, Stipetic, Agotic, or Brigadiers Gorinsek and Jezercic, and he believes that this is especially important to point out, and I agree with him. It is indeed very important to point out that Gorinsek is a Slovenian and Jezercic a Serb. I don't know whether Mr. Imre Agotic, the commander of the Croatian Air Force, is Hungarian or not. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: If I may say the following, that "Imre" is a Hungarian name, but of course the family name is not Hungarian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they are only my observations. I know the gentleman very well. However, we never asked -- I never asked him. I knew for some, but I don't know for him, I can't be sure of that. So this is more or less everything that merits mentioning from this article. There is a reference to the morale of the soldiers and all the factors that had a bearing on all of that. Can we now move on to the following one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The following is 3D01300. I suppose that you have not given up on the idea to present the first article, "Defence in the Service of the Civilian State." In e-court this is 329-0654.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it is 3D36-0765 through 0770.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an interview with the minister of defence, dated 28 January 1992. The title itself says that the defence of the state is in the service of a civilian state, which is very indicative. I'm going to skip the parts that concern the predictions of Mr. Susak with regard to the Blue Helmets, and I'm moving on to the part dealing with Bosnia and Herzegovina to question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just make an observation with regard to the transcript. The title of the article, as reproduced on page 53, lines 11 and 12, is: "Defence in the Service of the Civilian State in Electronic Courtroom," and that sounds very strange and must -- may well be something erroneous. Can we be told what the -- whether it is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The part about the electronic courtroom is superfluous. The title consists of just the initial few words. "Defence in the Service of the Civilian State" is the title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The journalist here asks about the possible continuation of a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a large contingent of the JNA arrives in Bosnia-Herzegovina from Slovenia and Croatia, the international community had permitted them to do so, and it says here that the situation in that Republic of the former Yugoslavia is getting worse. And he asks how will the Croatian defence react in case there's a conflict breaking out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The minister says that he is very worried, that Bosnia-Herzegovina is his original homeland, and he uses the following sentence: "We respected the requests of the international community about the non-violability of the borders and the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the other states which wish to be sovereign. We are not advocating the breakup or the carving up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Muslims, Serbs, and Croats are the constituent peoples of that republic. We respect their right to decide on their destiny themselves." There are talks about a possible referendum. He says at that moment he was not sure whether a referendum will be possible or not, and he goes on to say this: "The international community should be more involved in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If all three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina vote in favour of a sovereign and independent state, the Republic of Croatia will fully respect that." He goes on to say that obviously we will cooperate in economic, cultural and other terms, and everything else that goes with that. Another option would be to have cantons, to have a confederation. However, the general position of Croatia is that whatever is agreed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia will respect that, it will respect its territorial integrity. And he says as well if it comes to the worst, you have to have an "if" in politics. So if the Serbs take the position that Bosnia-Herzegovina must be carved up, and then if the Muslims also adopt that position, then the Croats will have to look after their own interests and make a decision accordingly. These "ifs" were misinterpreted in so many cases, although it is so clear, it is crystal clear, that if the Serbs take a position, if the Muslims take a position, it is only normal that Croats as well would take a position, but we will not be the first one to take such a position. The first position is the one that is discussed at all levels. I have a book showing what the government said at the time, what the parliament said at the time, and they all said the same thing. And he goes on to say this: "Croatia will not do anything to incite such an outcome. We want all three nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina to express their wishes democratically as to what kind of a state they wish to live in." What kind of a state, not which state. They can't opt to live in Croatia. They have to express a wish to live in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they also have to say what kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina they want to live in. He goes on to consider possible options. Your Honours, we simply knew, when the story was completed and when the indictment was on the table against Bosnia-Herzegovina which did nothing to the effect of the secession, the force of America says, Okay, we will give the Republika Srpska, which had done what it had done, which now lacks about half a million people who were not Serbs, here you had a state of your own. In Croatia, which pursued such a peaceful policy, together with its President Franjo Tudjman, they prepared the Plan Z-4 in which they offered the insurgent Serbs, after all the destructions and expulsions of all non-Serbs, in this Plan Z-4, America, France, England and Germany proposed for the Serbs in the occupied areas, as you can see them here [indicates], to be given a parliament -- their own tender, their own police. The only thing that they wouldn't have would be a ministry of foreign affairs and a military. The position was simply to put pressure on the weaker one and the more cooperative one and then charge him with all the evil. And finally the political options of foreigners were what they were. I can't deal with that at any great length. What I can say, that those political options were not moral, they were rather amoral, and my opinion will not be swayed in any direction in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, when you started talking about this article, you did not state the time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, I did state the time. The 28th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I can answer the question. And Susak, who went to study in Rijeka after completing high school, and he was persecuted by the regime because he shared the same -- we were classmates for six years, and we were close friends as children. We sat in the same -- at the same desk for two or three years. He then emigrated to Canada a long time ago, and then he came back as a man who -- well, he simply speaks about the possible policy that might be pursued by the USA. He speaks about the impact of the US business sphere, and he says it is the misfortune of small peoples, including Croatia, that their fate depends on such policies. And then he goes on to say this is not the first time that they supported dictators up until the very last moment, and then overnight they reversed their policies. I mean -- I'm talking about Cuba, Somosa, the Iranian Shah. I'm not going to talk about morality of the world politics, but the world politics and the international community and their policies should not bring us here under this indictment, because there's something terribly wrong here. So that's it about this article. Now we move on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next issue of "Hrvatski Vojnik" is from February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me come back to Mr. Susak. I believe his interview could be looked at through the premise of the JCE. In this interview, he addresses the question of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he seems to say that there are two possible solutions, two options, the first one being the following: Bosnia-Herzegovina, after a referendum, could become a state, with its three constitutive people, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, so he mentions this very clearly, and then he says there's a second possibility for solving the problem would be to set up a confederation, and then he addresses the problem of a confederation. So there's two options that are dealt with. Was this shared by all members of the government, by those who voted for the HZD, or was his personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: HDZ, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I think that this is not his view, what he would like to do. He says, We are going to accept everything that the peoples down there agree to. I will now speak very calmly. From this sentence, where it says, We depend on the solutions that will be brought up by the great powers, this is our fate, we always tried to divine what the intentions of the great powers were, and we tried to adapt to their proposals. So if they say a referendum, then we say, Okay, we'll have a referendum. If they say federation, we agree. And if they say cantons, we agree. If they say confederation, we agree. What I felt we could not agree to was that Bosnia and Herzegovina to become part of Serbia. I, personally - I'm now speaking for myself - I would not be able to accept this kind of solution, regardless of the consequences. Here we have some examples of what it looks like. I'm not going to be offering any value judgements here. So when Milosevic rescinded the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina, the autonomy where a large number of Hungarians participated in in Vojvodina, nobody said a word from the international community. He tore down the constitution of the state, he tore down the constitution of the state, because at that time they were interested in keeping Yugoslavia together. Fifteen years later, or ten years later, when Kosovo rebelled - I'm not going to say that I'm against Kosovo separating - America said, Well, we're not interested in the fact that you're a state and that there is a resolution of the UN Security Council guaranteeing your territorial integrity - now I'm talking about Serbia - we're going to launch air-strikes and we're going to grant Kosovo its independence. So this policy changed in the course of ten years, and we simply don't know what was cooking there. So this is not what we want. We are keeping a finger on the pulse. We know what we wanted. We wanted to have cantons. Well, apart from the basic prerogatives of the state, to have a high degree of decentralisation. Our main model was Switzerland, Switzerland, Switzerland. So there are three peoples, three religions. Let us come up with a model that would function seamlessly. Let us simply copy that model. Why should we invent a new model? That was our position, the position taken by Minister Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the indictment and in the preliminary brief, the Prosecutor writes the following in the pre-trial brief. He says that Tudjman and all those who took part in the JCE were playing a double game, if I could say so, which means that, on the one hand, they were saying that they respected the borders, that they respected the decisions made by the international community while pursuing their objective, which is annexation. This is at least what is alleged in the pre-trial brief, as well as in the indictment. I'm sure that during the cross-examination, he will come back to this issue. Well, in Mr. Susak's interview, he says the following, and I would like to shed some light on this in regards to the indictment. He says, We're not able to influence the politics of the other republics, notably the politics of Serbia. We can -- we do not claim the territory of the other republics where Croats actually live. This is very clear. He is saying that there is no territorial claim regarding the other republics. He mentions two examples, the city of Subotica. Very well. So this could be part of this double game. Here, very clearly, he states that the Republic of Croatia does not intend to annex anything or anyone, and then he continues by saying it's finally up to the Croats, if need be, to move from where they are, it's up to them to do this. Now, here's my question: You know Mr. Susak. You were schoolmates with him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That's what you told us, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to know whether he was able to actually use this double language. I'm talking here about Mr. Susak and not yourself, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reject -- I rule out any possibility, first of all, because I know him personally. And secondly, Your Honours, let us go back to real life. How can -- how can one think -- this is what I've already said. Well, we would have had to be total idiots, divorced from any kind of rational mindset, to sign -- for this government to sign all the resolutions of the UN Security Council, to let the UN in, to sign all the agreements, yes, to get into all this trouble about these territories, and then we were supposed to cheat the English, the French, the Americans, the Germans, and all the others. I really can't -- I have this problem here to keep the last vestiges of my rational mindset here. I really don't mind the trial, I don't mind the detention. My problem here is that I have to be an idiot. How can we -- how can we sign -- be admitted into the United Nations, sign all the conventions at the London Conference? I've said this 100 times. How can we take it, from whom, with what army? We are disarming, we are reorganising our armed forces. I simply cannot even conceive how somebody could say that. What kind of a double game? What would Gojko Susak take, with what? We are still trying to fight over whether we are going to -- we're going to -- we have to quarrel whether we're going to put the Croatian flag up at Prevlaka. First of all, it's simply not correct to assist the state, to take in so many people. What kind of a double game? I simply don't understand. Well, you're saying let's put a hypothetical question. Let's take this as a hypothesis: I want to play a double game and Gojko Susak wants to play a double game. Now, I want somebody to tell me what cards should I play, what documents, what instruments, what armed forces. I want somebody to tell me. I want somebody to tell me what should this single step be that we should take. Let me repeat, Your Honours. Franjo Tudjman agreed to this Z-4 plan. The proposal was for the Glina district and for the Knin district to be autonomous district with a Serb majority. I do apologise. They should have their own police. They should be autonomous within Croatia. We will go back -- we will go back to those texts a little while later. So within Croatia, he agrees to this, plan Z-4, where this area -- this area here and this area there [indicates] are to be considered as a single whole inhabited by Serbs, who should have their own police, their own money. Z-4 was put forward by Galbraith, France, England and Germany, and Martic was the one to reject it because that was too little for him. And now this politician and this policy that is pursued within Croatia regarding the areas from which Croats were expelled, now -- these politicians should now play a game that would aim at the separation of these areas as well. I really can't understand it. I am really struggling to keep my rationality here. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. General Praljak spoke too fast, and the last sentence got lost in translation. At page 62, lines 10, 11, and 12, Mr. Praljak said that: "Now this kind of state is supposed to have as its goal the separation of parts -- or the secession of parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not of Croatia inhabited by Serbs." Perhaps he should repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do so. I will be a little bit calmer, and I have to apologise to Your Honours for being emotional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, one last question before the break. You spoke about the Z-4 plan. You said that in this plan, President Tudjman would accept, more or less, that part of the Croatian territory would be inhabited by Serbs, who would have their own lists and so on. Could you tell us what was the impact of the Z-4 plan among the population? Did people think it was normal or was it a subject of debate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, President Tudjman accepted the Z-4 plan. He accepted the Z-4 plan, which contained the provisions that the occupied parts of the Republic of Croatia, from which Serbs had expelled the non-Serb populations, destroyed non-Serb houses, and killed 600 civilians in that area while UNPROFOR was deployed there, and in spite of all that four countries, America, Germany, France and England, put Tudjman in front of a fait accompli to give to those areas -- Martic and Babic the kind of autonomy where they would have everything except for the foreign policy and the armed forces. They would have government, money, the police force and so on. I was desolate, I have to say. I was really dismayed, and I did not agree with this decision by President Tudjman. There you have it. But I want to say that leniency went that far. In my case, I thought it was too much. I was opposed to it. But then if you have this man who accepted that -- and Gojko Susak and the government accepted all that. To accuse him that he's trying to play some games behind the scenes against this powerful international community in order to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina, well, that's -- really, that goes beyond any kind of rational thought, the kind of rational thinking that I have. But in my testimony, I will show why this was the case. The Serbs were offering that. They were saying, Franjo, You can have Western Herzegovina and you can give us the rest and these parts here, [indicates], and then everything is going to be peaceful and quiet, and that's -- Alija Izetbegovic was also offering, You can take Western Herzegovina with you and then we will deal with the Serbs, we will deal with them. These were the proposals, and I will show that beyond any doubt these were the proposals made by the Serb and the Muslim side. That was the way that Bosnia was being destroyed and carved up. Never, ever -- I will show statements by the highest officials by the international community confirming that I am telling the truth, including General Klein and all the others. Alija Izetbegovic personally told him he had made those proposals to Franjo Tudjman, and this is, in logical terms, a swap of the premises. Never, ever, Your Honours. This was not on the table at all. This was out of the question. But I will show later who proposed the reallocation of the population. We'll show that. That's why I wanted to take up so much of my time to testify here before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's break. It's 20 after 12.00, and we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, let's go to 3D01301 now, please, and there's an article there about Daidza. It was mentioned several times during these proceedings, "Daidza Defends the Homeland," and perhaps we can use this opportunity to explain who the individual is. E-court number is 3D29-0657, and the translation is 3D36-771 to 773. Go ahead, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Daidza emigrated to America straight away, I believe 1945, and he returned, as he said, in February 1991. Now, regardless of the fact that his name, first name is Mato, he's in fact a Muslim, and he was the commander of Krajl Tomislav unit, which was in the HVO, and you'll be able to see from the documents that he had a whole series of meetings and talks with Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Izetbegovic in fact was -- sent some orders to that unit. At the beginning of the war, it was a unit manned by more Croats than Muslims, but as the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina intensified, he let people from his unit go, or rather weapons too, or rather he sent the Muslims fight where the danger from the Yugoslav Peoples' Army was worse. But I want to stress something he says, and he says that he gathered together a number of young people, young men around him - that's in response to the first question - and there were more and more volunteers with each passing day. So it was the volunteers who joined up as the war intensified. And he says, We had neither weapons, nor equipment, and the young men kept coming and brought with them weapons that they had procured themselves. He goes on to say that he trained the fighters illegally and that an attack on Dubrovnik was not expected. And he goes on to say that the unit took part in the fighting on the whole theatre of operation in Southern Dalmacija theatre of war, Osojnik, Cepikuce, Ston, the hills around Konavle, and so on. And he says that there weren't many professionals, that there was a lot of fear, that they hadn't been prepared properly, and he says, How are you going to send a child of 19 out there, dress him in a uniform and put boots on his feet, and send him out to man some positions in the evening? And then he comes to something important and says that they were attacked by the Chetniks and that they were looting all over the place, and he says that the fighters took this badly, of course, and wanted to advance on Trebinje. And he became a general of the Croatian Army later on and he says, I prevented this, it's not something that existed in our parts, blood-feud and taking revenge. There were mistakes, there were, of course, heroes who found me tedious with all my preaching. And then he goes on to say that everybody who knew what the situation looked like -- well, he says too much blood was shed, there are too many graves, that he would often criticise his soldiers and then kiss them and embrace them, and that you had to be a father to the troops as well when you had such young men in your midst, and that he viewed every soldier as his very own son. And he says that he would have been happiest had they been able to fight using just pens and computers. So on the Croatian side, there were generals and officers -- well, nobody wanted to go to war for its own sake. They went to war just because they couldn't allow anybody to trample their country and dignity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, General, was he also one of those people who first fought in Croatia and then later on went to Bosnia, because that's not contained in this article, but was that the case with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was involved over there, and when the plan to lift the siege of Sarajevo was put in place, he was appointed commander. Mr. Izetbegovic appointed him commander, in fact. He was in command of operations against the Chetniks throughout the Neretva River valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I think that we can move on now to the next document of "Hrvatski Vojnik." 3D01302 is the number, and I think you wanted to tell us something about the first article entitled "The Winner is the Croatian People." 3D29-0659 is the number, and in English it is 3D36-774 and 775.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a meeting between the supreme commander and the Croatian Army officers. Dr. Franjo Tudjman here is speaking about -- well, he's informing the officers of how they'll be trained and educated, and he told them of the arrival of the international forces, and how they were to be welcomed, and the duties they were to perform. And at the end, it says that the president drew the attention for need for the arrival of the Blue Helmets or international forces, and he advocates their arrival. And I know for certain that he always advocated that. He was happiest if the Blue Helmets arrived and deployed along Croatia's borders. He didn't succeed in that, and he says the adversary still has strong weapons at his disposal and can do a lot more damage. And he says that Croatia would not have received international recognition had we not agreed to the peace efforts, but he also says that if all else fails, we must be ready to achieve peace through our own forces. And that's what happened. The Z-4 failed and all other attempts failed, and then with the political action underway, we gained the right to liberate certain parts of Croatia by a police and military operation. And here it's important to note that the president says that he has decided to demobilise, first of all, 20.000 HVO members, HVO soldiers, and that in the second stage of the demobilisation the remaining half be halved. So 20.000 to begin with, and then as soon as that was done, that the remaining number should be halved again. And he goes on to say that to continue the war, we will not need such a large army, and that it is an unbearable burden placed on the Croatian economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You meant the HV?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the HV. So these are clear-cut messages about Croatian policy, through an explanation given by someone who was the number-one man, and that was Dr. Franjo Tudjman. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For the record, on page 68, line 2, it says "HVO members" twice. The general is expressly talking about HV, the Croatian Army here. Now, General, the next document is 3D01303, and that is the first article -- well, the first article follows on from the topic that you mentioned, the deployment of the UN forces in Croatia and so on, so on the eve of their deployment. And the date is the 8th of April, 1992, of this particular edition.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have anything much to add, just to say that this article gives the correct overview as to the deployment of the United Nations peacekeeping forces in Croatia and which areas were considered north, east, south and west, Sector North, Sector South, et cetera. And then he mentions the commands of the international forces. So that's what that's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, just one question in this regard. You referred a number of times to the map behind you. Now, those zones are covered by the areas that you demonstrated on the map; right? For the record, I'm referring to the article that begins on 3D29-0661, and in English, 3D36-1050 to 1053. We can move on to the next document, which is 3D01304, "Hrvatski Vojnik," dated the 5th of June, 1992, and I think you might want to comment on this article titled "The Croatian Army - The Pillar of the Croatian State-Building Idea." In e-court, it is 3D29-0664, and in English it is 3D36-0776 to 779. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the solemn oath-taking before Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the supreme commander, that was taken only then by the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff, and the officers of the Croatian Army and Air Force, and I'd like to stress here -- they pledged their allegiance, and I'd like to stress the part of the article where the president says that once again they found that the will of the people cannot be quashed, a people who have, who are fully conscious that the historical moment has come for them to gain their full independence and liberty. And he once again underlines the importance of international relations, and I quote: "By becoming a member of the United Nations organisation, with its admission to membership of the United Nations, Croatia has become an equal member of the free, sovereign and independent states of the world, and from these foundations it will be easier for us to finish the war which was imposed on us, also in terms of international law and not just in military terms. It is upon these foundations that we shall be able to devote ourselves to building our homeland as of tomorrow." So the man who had already experienced a war and who was a historian, and knew exactly what it meant to be a member of the United Nations, what it meant to sign the international covenant and agreement. So even the smallest -- minutest possibility can be refuted that he would do something in the background to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's something that is absolutely inconceivable of a man like that, just as inconceivable as if you were to say that the green tangent is singing. Next he goes on to say that we must be wise and build up an army, the kind of army that we really need and meets our requirements, not to burden the Croatian economy. And in another excerpt, he said that we should demobilise a significant portion -- well, even the largest portion of the Croatian Army, bearing in mind, at the same time, the interests of the state and the economy as a whole, but that we should leave behind professional, capable military units. So the overall leadership already at that time was turned towards peace. They had their eyes on peace, demobilisation, the prevention of the country's further destruction, et cetera, the development of the economy. And that's what I have to say about that article.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next article in the same issue is under the title "Croatia Surrounded by the World." 3D29-0666 is the number of the article, and in English it is 3D36-779 to 781. The author is Davor Butkovic. Do you wish to address that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the editors say here that before the last issue went to print, 757 Security Council resolution was passed imposing strict sanctions against the SFRY-SRY, the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, and that this news confirms the assertions set out in this article. And here -- that's from the editorial board, and here's what Mr. Butkovic says in his article: He is writing the article at the time they were celebrating the entry of the Tigers, the 1st Brigade of the Croatian Army, into Dubrovnik, whereby the process of liberating the occupied parts of the country had finally begun, and he says that this did not reverberate in the public, that not enough publicity was given to the visit of several representatives from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank who discussed how to provide financial aid to Croatia with the government and national bank officials. They did not receive much public attention. He says that loans could be expected, financial aid in general, and he considered that this was equally important, as was the liberation of Dubrovnik, and shows the full importance of Croatia's admission into the United Nations. And further down the text, he makes an analysis of relations with the MMF, UNESCO and so on and so forth -- IMF and UNESCO, et cetera, and everything that was being done in that area for the integration of Croatia into international institutions, and says that as far as Croatians are concerned, and I quote: "For Croatia, membership into the United Nations laid the foundations and prerequisites for the successful use of otherwise favourable international opinion and international climate, which will best benefit a depleted economy." He analyses the problems very well and looks at how Yugoslavia, before Croatia was accepted into UN membership -- well, Croatia did not sign anything before it was received into the United Nations family, and that is why it is in a far better position simply because the occupied territories in UN -- in the focus of UN attention were in Croatia's possession, and for the fact that Croatia need not strike any agreement in which the status of those areas is determined negatively, as far as our state interests are concerned. Up until Croatia's membership and admission to the United Nations, Yugoslavia was the only country that had the right to sign a state agreement with that world organisation, which means that it made decisions on the status of the occupied territories. That is now legally and formally impossible. And he goes on to say that the other tactical advantage that Croatia had, which was key after being admitted into the United Nations, is the fact that it had the possibility of being invited to the 7th Chapter -- or, rather, the protection that the world organisation provides to countries exposed to attack, and says, and I quote: "All further UN resolutions on Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia will be taken probably within the context of Chapter 7." Once again, it was brought to light that Croatia, by requesting admission into all international institutions, recognises the international order and hopes that that international order, and here we have Chapter 7 mentioned, will be used as aid and assistance both to Croatia and to Bosnia-Herzegovina so that the imposed war can be resolved with the help of the United Nations. Unfortunately, the aid and assistance that we had expected to receive was found short, which then led to all the things that happened and that we know about. The war continued, chaos continued, nobody was able to tackle the chaos, and then individual crimes that were committed during that same war. That's all for me on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If we can move to 3D01 -- there's a question coming from one of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would only simply like to say that of course it is a very interesting article which was written by Davor Butkovic, and I followed it with interest and read it. On the other hand, of course, I have to say that it was a bit -- a rosy interpretation of what happened when -- it was, of course, very important that Croatia has become a UN member, and it should be underlined. On the other hand, of course, Chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter, as we all know, I believe, could only be evoked and utilised if the Security Council itself is going to make a determination that there was a fact which would threaten international peace and security, because the whole meaning of Chapter 7 is based on that very notion. So, therefore, I think as the -- firstly, as the events showed themselves at a later stage as well, although the admission of Croatia to the UN was a very important step indeed, on the other hand I would say that it didn't solve all the problems, as we all know, and therefore the reference to this editorial or to this article is although important, but again I would say that it was not the final panacea for Croatia. On the other hand, it is also true that the Resolution of the Security Council 757, which is also referred to in this article, it was very important because it really imposed strict sanctions against, at that time, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, we can go back to the number that I just called, 3D01 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour. I believe that he expresses his hope in the article. It was not an assertion, but rather a hope. He didn't know, as we didn't know, what would happen. He -- that's why he expresses his hope. Go on, you can proceed, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's deal with 3D01305. I suppose that you wanted to say something about this short article. In e-court, the number is 3D29-0669, and in English it is 3D36-782.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a number of text that I wanted to comment. However, I don't have the time. I just wanted to list them, I'm going to read their titles, and you're going to provide us with the numbers. It says here that Croatia supports war crimes investigations. In the following text -- this is said by Mate Granic, who was the minister of foreign affairs and vice-president of the government at the time. In the following text, an explanation is provided as to the nature of war crimes. It is provided in somewhat greater detail. And then the following text says that a new Nuremberg trial is in the offing, and it is also said that a special commission of the United Nations, before the end of January 1993, will submit to the Secretary-General a whole file with the war crimes that had been investigated. In the following text, it says that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for the interruption. I'm having trouble following, and I'm not sure whether the general's moving on to subsequent exhibits that have different exhibit numbers, with the intention to come back to the numbers later, but it's hard to follow and I'm a bit lost, I guess. And if we could give the number at the time he's talking about a specific exhibit, it would be helpful, I think, just not for me but for the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my learned friend. We are still dealing with the same exhibit, which is 3D01305. And after the first article that you must have seen on the screen, the general wants to proceed and list the titles found in the document dealing with the same subject. The number is 3D36-0783 and the page after -- the pages that follow. I can give you their numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take things at a time. "What are War Crimes" is the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read. We will read much faster if I read all the numbers. The next one is 3D40-0911. This is the English version. 3D40-0912, 3D40-0913, and then through 0920. And we're going to hear only the titles from the general, who wants to show that what Mr. Granic is saying in the first article makes all the sense in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following text explains the nature of war crimes, what they are, indeed. At least that's how I read the article, or at least that's the perception of the author. The Geneva Conventions are referred to in here, and so on and so forth. In the following text, it says that a new Nuremberg trial is in the offing, and a reference is made to the existing trial, the trial that we are sitting at here today, which would try for war crimes committed during the war. And information is provided as to what is going on. And the following text says that a quest was launched for -- or, rather, a hunt was launched for war criminals, and you can see that there are pictures of Milosevic, Karadzic, Mladic, Arkan, and Seselj. Also, it says that a decision was issued by the Security Council to establish a commission for war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, and that it immediately embarked upon collecting documentation about war crimes. And the following text says that there is a mounting body of evidence about war crimes, and it says here that British Television faced Arkan with some of the witnesses' testimonies and the photos of his atrocities. And the representative of the French government, after having toured the Serb concentration camps in Bosnia and Herzegovina, claims that he already has the names of 11 Serb war crimes. At the end of that article, we see this text, the recognition of Serbian war crime, and it says that Borislav Herak admitted to an American journalist that he, himself, had killed 29 people and testified to -- witnessed the killing of 250 men, that he participated in torture, rape, and plunder, and that he -- and that that was published by journalist Barnes in "The New York Times," and the title of that article was "A Story of a Murderer." The following article explains that genocide is the gravest of crimes, and again there is a discussion about a Greater Serbia and its borders along the Karlobag-Karlovac-Sisak-Virovitica line, and that Vojislav Seselj was one of the key players who supported that idea. And then the following page provides a list of what is going on. Italians and French supported the establishment of an international tribunal is one of the things that is happening. And then what Giuliano Amato, the Italian prime minister, stated in London. And then it says that a centre of human rights was established in Zagreb. Again, reference is made to that centre, which shouldn't close its eyes before the Serbian crimes committed in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is also official data about the crimes committed in Croatia. It says here that Clinton is also in favour of a new Nuremberg trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that my learned friend was now able to follow, or if not, a majority of the English translations are enclosed with 3D01993. It's the -- it is the same issue of "Hrvatski Vojnik." The translations are there, and I apologise if you had problems following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, the following is 3D01 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going to skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You want to go to 994; okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is what I meant. I thought that you might want to skip that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a follow-up question. You have just read out the article that mentions crimes and announces that there may be, in the future, a tribunal. Earlier on, you spoke about Resolution 757, which gave my fellow Judge the opportunity to intervene. I hesitated because I was waiting for the right moment to do so, and the right moment is now with this document. As you know, and you demonstrated this, you read the resolution which is but the follow-up of Resolution 752 which was not implemented, therefore there was a need for a new resolution, which asked the states to comply with resolutions. It was, among other things, asked of the Army of Croatia that it should leave the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was also asked of the neighbours of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to interfere within the boundaries of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So at the very moment when the resolutions were adopted, at the very moment when Chapter 7 was mentioned, at the level of the Croatian Army, was there an assessment of the situation in order to see in what field the Croatian Army was to criticise itself or investigate itself so that some day it would avoid falling under a resolution that would criticise or condemn specific types of behaviour? You were a general, among other generals of the Croatian Army. Did you assess the situation? Did you see whether there was a potential risk that one day you might have to respond, answer to crimes that you could be charged with, or did nobody take that into account ? You were one of the key players at the time. Therefore, it might be interesting to hear you on this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, Your Honours, from the very arrival you've seen, and you will see from my behaviour in Sunja, from the very outset I tried to teach them about everything that is contained in the International Law of War. We continuously, in continuum, without any interruptions, educated every Croatian soldier as to what they could do and what they shouldn't do, and this did not stop for a single moment. When I complete this, I'm going to show you a text that I, myself, sent to the Croatian Army from the IPD Department. In that text, I tell them this: Gentlemen, you will not be exculpated from a single crime you may commit, be it looting or something else. You will not be tried less because of the fact you are Croatian soldiers. You will be tried even more. You will see the document. It was not on the list because it was not translated on time. I also deal with the law, and I quote from the Penal Code and tell them how much they can expect for each of the crimes they may commit. I tell them also, Gentlemen, we are fighting for a state with a rule of law, and you can rest assured that you will be convicted. There is the document there [indicates]. This is the one that I'm discussing, if I may be provided the document. Not for a single moment, therefore. And you have also seen this from the Prosecutor's submission, how many people were actually processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Usher, please, your help is required.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many people were processed, how many people had criminal proceedings instituted against them. Your Honours, we were absolutely convinced that we would be able to process not everybody; certain things will remain unpunished. However, our instinct was to process everybody. As far as the part concerning the withdrawal of the Croatian Army from Bosnia and Herzegovina, that resolution was passed based on incorrect, false, and propaganda thesis that were proposed by the Serbs, by some members of the international community, and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. There were no members of the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, save for those that I already mentioned. I know that. I know those who came by name. I knew all the volunteers by name and by face, each and every one of them. When I come to that, when I start explaining the situation down there, I'm going to give you their names, their family names, where they hailed from, what their mothers and fathers did for a living. I can tell you that about most of the people who came down there to fight on the side of the Croatian Army. There was a story going around about several brigades, maybe five or six, of the Croatian Army in Central Bosnia, and at one point Mr. Alija Izetbegovic accused Franjo Tudjman, but that was a pure and simple propaganda lie. There were no Croatian soldiers in Central Bosnia; maybe there were 10 or 12 volunteers from the Croatian Army, and that's all. But let me go back to the document dated 1 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 3D03316. This has not been translated. It was on our last submission to be added to the 65 ter list. However, it was turned down, together with many others, because they were not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll find a way. The text is long. I signed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If it's not on the 65 ter list, if it's not translated, then we object to it's being used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you might use this document later on, when it will be translated. You've heard the objection from Mr. Stringer. I'm sure later on you'll have the opportunity to come back to this, and when we all have that document translated it will be better. It's not that we don't trust you, but it's much easier for each and every one to have the translated document at hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, just two short parts from the beginning, very short parts, just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The Prosecution objects and asks that the witness follow the Trial Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next time, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us move on, then. 3D001995. It's a text about the third anniversary of the first convention of the HDZ. "Every Drop of Croatian Blood is Sacred." Mr. Kovacic, could you please just read the reference for the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, it appears that there is some confusion with the English documents. We have another English document attached to this one, and I don't have it here. In Croatian, that would be 3D30-0122. That's the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, General, we can skip this one and leave it for tomorrow, because we have to verify what's happened.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. But we have this "One Year of the Military Prosecutors Office."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, this one has a translation. It's 3D40-0801. That's the English translation. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we have a brief text about the military public prosecutors -- military prosecutors office. And here we can see what has been done, and I note that the military prosecutor, Colonel Mirsad Baksic, is a Muslim. And it is important to note that nobody will get away with impunity, and nobody who has done something will go unpunished, and the Croatian judiciary does not blame ethnic communities as wholes for crimes. And this is the only way that the functioning of the legal system in Croatia will be guaranteed is through vigorous prosecution. That's all I have about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's "One Year of Military Prosecutors Office." It's 3D31-0024, that's the Croatia version, and 3D40-0801, that's the English version. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, the exhibit number for that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Exhibit number was 001995. Yes, I'm sorry, one 0 too much. That was 019955.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, General, is "Hrvatski Vojnik" from March 1993, 3D01996. Which articles did you want to speak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Second Chamber of the Croatian Parliament Set Up."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's 3D31-0026, that's the Croatia version in e-court, and the English version is 3D40-0803 and the pages that follow.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like now to focus once again to the address by President Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and I would start from where it says: "Serbs and UNPROFOR," where he again speaks about the role and what we sought from the international community, and how UNPROFOR came to be deployed, and he says that about 22 per cent of the Croatian territory is still held by the insurgents. And he says, according to the 1991 census, there were 520.000 Serbs living in Croatia or some 10 per cent of the population, and in their key districts, Glina and Knin -- Knin and Glina, which covered 12.55 per cent of the Croatian territory, there was a total of 4 per cent of the Croatian population living there. Furthermore, from the overall number of Serbs in Croatia before the aggression, in the area covered by the present districts, 24.8 per cent of Serbs lived there. So a bit less than a quarter of all Serbs lived in those districts. So the aggression that was launched was not launched solely to protect Serbs, because most of the Serbs in Croatia lived in Zagreb, in Rijeka, in Istria and so on. They simply wanted to carve the state of Croatia up in an area where only 24 per cent of the overall number of Serbs lived. The remaining Serbs in Croatia lived as Croatian citizens, they served in the Croatian Army, they did their jobs, and they suffered the same fate as everybody else. Dr. Franjo Tudjman goes on to say, in an effort to avoid further war victims, the Croatian policy wants to garner the aid of the international community to achieve an end to the Serbian aggression against Croatia. He goes on to say that the population living in those areas find their lives unbearable, the conditions of life for most people living there are intolerable, and the ringleaders of the insurgency do not have the right to speak on behalf of the majority of the Serbs living in other areas in Croatia. And he goes on to say that it is encouraging that numerous initiatives are cropping up on the Serb side in UNPA areas. Of course, Dr. Franjo Tudjman had one man, Slavko Degoricija, in the government, who was in charge of the talks with the Serbs, and I think that he had more than 150 meetings with him. In particular, the talks with this area around Okucani and Gracanica were fruitful, and I have to say that the Serb leaders in this area are today, and in fact immediately after the liberation of that area, became members of the Croatian Parliament, so those people who created this state within a state in Croatia, they today sit in the Croatian Parliament. They were not tried, they were not punished because they had not committed any war crimes. Croatia did not try to impose any kind of collective blame, as the military prosecutor noted, and as soon as things were back to normal they rejoined the normal political life in Croatia. Furthermore, Franjo Tudjman says that they will persevere in pursuing this policy, that all loyal citizens of Croatia will have their civil and human rights guaranteed. The right to local self-government according to the highest standards in Europe and the developed world will be guaranteed. So offering all political preconditions for the normalisation of the relations, we have to draw the attention to the fact that we will also persevere on holding responsible under the law those who committed war crimes and those who continue committing war crimes and atrocities and ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 1.45 and we have to put an end to this today. I'm sure we'll continue tomorrow with the same document, if Mr. Kovacic still has questions to put on this document. As you know, we're sitting in the morning at 9.00. I adjourn for the day. I wish you a fine afternoon, and we'll reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
